title: AI Office Interim Guidance 01/2025 — GPAI Transparency
text:
# AI Office Interim Guidance 01/2025 — GPAI Transparency

**Date:** February 7, 2025
**Author:** AI Office (interim)

Interim Guidance 01/2025 on the transparency and technical-documentation obligations of general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers under the AI Act. On an interim basis, providers should maintain transparency documentation limited to a model card and a summary of training-data sources; the fuller technical documentation set (evaluation and systemic-risk assessment) is described as forthcoming in a later Annex-style technical file. This is the interim position on GPAI provider transparency and technical-documentation obligations under the AI Office guidance, pending the final guidance, and may change.

title: AI Office Guidance 04/2025 — GPAI Transparency (Final)
text:
# AI Office Guidance 04/2025 — GPAI Transparency (Final)

**Date:** September 22, 2025
**Author:** AI Office

Final Guidance 04/2025 on GPAI provider transparency obligations under the AI Act. Providers must keep the full technical documentation set (model card, training-data summary, evaluation and systemic-risk assessment where applicable) and make it available to the AI Office on request. This Guidance 04/2025 supersedes and replaces the Interim Guidance 01/2025 of 7 February 2025; the interim 'forthcoming technical file' position no longer applies. This is the current binding guidance for GPAI transparency.

title: NIS2 Incident-Reporting — Compliance Position v1 (CS-NIS2-07)
text:
# NIS2 Incident-Reporting — Compliance Position v1 (CS-NIS2-07)

**Date:** January 15, 2024
**Author:** Northwind Security & Compliance

Compliance position v1 assessing our NIS2 incident-notification duty as of this date. Our reading of the incident-reporting timeline under CS-NIS2-07: for any significant incident, file a single full incident report with the national CSIRT within 72 hours of becoming aware; no separate early-warning step is required. This is the incident-reporting timeline we follow under our NIS2 standard — standing assessment pending the next review.

title: NIS2 Incident-Reporting & 24h Early Warning — Compliance Position v2 (CS-NIS2-07)
text:
# NIS2 Incident-Reporting & 24h Early Warning — Compliance Position v2 (CS-NIS2-07)

**Date:** March 11, 2025
**Author:** Northwind Security & Compliance

Compliance position v2 reassessing our NIS2 incident-notification duty. Current reading: submit an early warning to the national CSIRT within 24 hours of becoming aware, then a full notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month. The standard sets the duty and the deadlines; it does not name the specific submission channel or endpoint to use with the national CSIRT — see operational guidance. Position v2 replaces v1 of 15 January 2024; the prior single-72-hour-report reading is no longer current. This is our current assessment of the incident-reporting obligation.

title: International Transfers — Compliance Position v1 (DT-03)
text:
# International Transfers — Compliance Position v1 (DT-03)

**Date:** March 3, 2023
**Author:** Northwind Data Protection Office

Compliance position v1 assessing our approach to transfers of personal data to third countries. Reading: execute the legacy controller-to-processor standard contractual clauses (the 2010 set) and attach them to the data-processing agreement; no transfer impact assessment required. This standard-contractual-clause configuration is what our data-transfer policy DT-03 requires for transfers to third countries. Standing assessment for third-country transfers.

title: International Transfers — Compliance Position v2 (DT-03)
text:
# International Transfers — Compliance Position v2 (DT-03)

**Date:** August 19, 2025
**Author:** Northwind Data Protection Office

Compliance position v2 reassessing our approach to third-country transfers. Current reading: use the modular Commission standard contractual clauses, selecting the module matching the transfer role (e.g. Module Two for controller-to-processor), and complete a documented transfer impact assessment before the first transfer. title: Risk Classification — CV-Screening Assistant (Limited-Risk)

# Risk Classification — CV-Screening Assistant (Limited-Risk)

**Date:** May 14, 2024
**Author:** Northwind AI Governance Board

Classification opinion on the internal CV-Screening Assistant under the AI Act. Assessment of the AI Act risk classification of the CV-Screening Assistant: the tool only ranks and summarises applications for human reviewers and does not itself decide outcomes, so its risk classification is limited-risk, with transparency obligations only. title: Revised Risk Classification — CV-Screening Assistant (High-Risk, Annex III)
text:
# Revised Risk Classification — CV-Screening Assistant (High-Risk, Annex III)

**Date:** July 8, 2025
**Author:** Northwind AI Governance Board

Revised classification of the CV-Screening Assistant under the AI Act. On review, the tool is used in recruitment and materially influences shortlisting, so it falls under Annex III point 4 (employment / worker management) and is high-risk. A conformity assessment, risk-management system, logging and human-oversight measures are now required. This revised classification supersedes the limited-risk opinion of 14 May 2024, which is no longer valid. Current classification of record.

title: GDPR Article 6 — Lawfulness of Processing
text:
# GDPR Article 6 — Lawfulness of Processing

**Date:** May 25, 2018
**Author:** Official Journal (consolidated)

Article 6 GDPR. Processing is lawful only if at least one basis applies: (a) consent; (b) performance of a contract; (c) compliance with a legal obligation; (d) protection of vital interests; (e) a task in the public interest or official authority; (f) legitimate interests, balanced against the data subject's rights. These six lawful bases are a foundational provision of the Regulation; they are not altered by sectoral guidance or subsequent technical instruments.

title: NIS2 — Essential vs Important Entities (Scope Definitions)
text:
# NIS2 — Essential vs Important Entities (Scope Definitions)

**Date:** December 14, 2022
**Author:** Official Journal

Scope definitions under NIS2. The Directive distinguishes 'essential' entities (larger operators in the highest-criticality sectors, subject to ex-ante supervision) from 'important' entities (other in-scope operators, subject to ex-post supervision); both are determined by sector and size thresholds. These category definitions are structural to the Directive and are not changed by sectoral implementing acts.

title: AI Act Article 5 — Prohibited Practices (In Force)
text:
# AI Act Article 5 — Prohibited Practices (In Force)

**Date:** August 1, 2024
**Author:** Official Journal

Article 5 AI Act lists the prohibited AI practices in force: among them certain manipulative or exploitative techniques, untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases, social scoring by public authorities, and — subject to narrow law-enforcement exceptions — real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces. This is the prohibited-practices list currently in force.

title: Proposed Amendment — Add Workplace Emotion-Recognition Ban (WITHDRAWN)
text:
# Proposed Amendment — Add Workplace Emotion-Recognition Ban (WITHDRAWN)

**Date:** November 20, 2025
**Author:** (proposal, withdrawn)

Draft amendment proposing to extend the Article 5 AI Act prohibited-practices list — which prohibits manipulative or exploitative techniques, untargeted scraping of facial images, social scoring, and real-time remote biometric identification — with a blanket ban on emotion-recognition systems in the workplace. The draft states it 'would replace the current Article 5 list' once adopted. NOTE: this amendment was WITHDRAWN in committee and was never adopted; it has no legal effect and does not change the AI practices prohibited under Article 5.

title: DPIA Policy DP-02 — When a Data Protection Impact Assessment Is Required
text:
# DPIA Policy DP-02 — When a Data Protection Impact Assessment Is Required

**Date:** September 9, 2024
**Author:** Northwind Data Protection Office

Policy DP-02 implementing the GDPR DPIA duty. A DPIA is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals — in particular systematic and extensive profiling with significant effects, large-scale processing of special-category data, or large-scale systematic monitoring of a public area. When the screening thresholds are met, the DPIA precedes processing. Current standing policy.

title: Supervisory Authority A — Opinion 12/2025: Pseudonymised Telemetry Is Personal Data
text:
# Supervisory Authority A — Opinion 12/2025: Pseudonymised Telemetry Is Personal Data

**Date:** October 3, 2025
**Author:** Data Protection Authority A

Opinion 12/2025. Where a device-telemetry stream is keyed to a persistent pseudonymous identifier that the controller can re-link to an account, the data remain PERSONAL DATA: pseudonymisation reduces but does not remove identifiability. Such telemetry is therefore within the scope of the GDPR and needs an Article 6 basis.

title: Supervisory Authority B — Opinion 7/2025: Equivalent Telemetry Falls Outside the GDPR
text:
# Supervisory Authority B — Opinion 7/2025: Equivalent Telemetry Falls Outside the GDPR

**Date:** September 18, 2025
**Author:** Data Protection Authority B

Opinion 7/2025. Where device telemetry is aggregated and the linking keys are held only by a separate processor under contractual and technical separation, the controller's copy is effectively ANONYMOUS and falls OUTSIDE the GDPR; no Article 6 basis is required for it. This opinion concerns telemetry materially equivalent to that addressed by Authority A.

title: AI Office Q&A — Purely Internal Model Use Is Out of Scope of Provider Duties
text:
# AI Office Q&A — Purely Internal Model Use Is Out of Scope of Provider Duties

**Date:** April 16, 2025
**Author:** AI Office

Q&A clarification. An organisation that develops a model and uses it only internally, without placing it on the market or putting it into service for others, does NOT thereby take on the AI Act's provider obligations for that model; deployer duties may still apply. Purely internal development-and-use is outside the provider regime.

title: Client Alert — Internal-Only AI Models ARE In Scope as Provider Activity
text:
# Client Alert — Internal-Only AI Models ARE In Scope as Provider Activity

**Date:** May 6, 2025
**Author:** Outside Counsel (client alert)

Client alert. In our view any organisation that builds and runs its own AI model is acting as a provider and takes on the full AI Act provider obligations, including for purely internal deployments. Firms should assume internal-only models ARE in scope and prepare conformity documentation accordingly.

title: GDPR Article 83 — General Conditions for Administrative Fines
text:
# GDPR Article 83 — General Conditions for Administrative Fines

**Date:** May 25, 2018
**Author:** Official Journal (consolidated)

Article 83 GDPR sets the administrative-fine framework. The higher tier — up to EUR 20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher — applies to infringements of, among others, the basic principles for processing, the data-subject rights, and the rules on transfers of personal data to third countries. This is the binding statutory basis for the highest tier of administrative fines.

text:
# Blog — Is There a 'New' Seventh Lawful Basis in 2025?

**Date:** October 2, 2025
**Author:** vendor marketing blog

Marketing post claiming a brand-new 'legitimate-innovation' lawful basis for AI training has arrived in 2025 and supplements the GDPR's bases. This is not accurate — no such basis exists; Article 6 still sets out the six lawful bases. Lawful basis, consent, legitimate interests, AI training — fresh-dated but wrong.

**Date:** May 22, 2025
**Author:** trade news

title: Blog — GDPR Fines Explained: the Maximum Fine You Risk for Unlawful Transfers of Personal Data Outside the EU
text:
# Blog — GDPR Fines Explained: the Maximum Fine You Risk for Unlawful Transfers of Personal Data Outside the EU

**Date:** March 14, 2025
**Author:** industry blog

Plain-language explainer on GDPR fines and penalty ceilings: there are two tiers, the higher reaching the larger of EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover — the maximum fine you risk for the serious violations, including unlawful transfers of personal data outside the EU. Fine, penalty, ceiling, tier, turnover, 4%, 20 million, enforcement, transfer violations — a keyword-dense summary of how much you can be fined; readers always ask which provision sets the maximum fine they risk for an unlawful transfer of personal data outside the EU — useful background, not the binding legal text.

title: AI Act Annex III — High-Risk Use Cases (List)
text:
# AI Act Annex III — High-Risk Use Cases (List)

**Date:** August 1, 2024
**Author:** Official Journal

Annex III AI Act enumerates high-risk use cases, including: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education; employment and worker management (point 4); access to essential private and public services and benefits, including creditworthiness (point 5); law enforcement; migration; and administration of justice. Inclusion in Annex III, absent a narrow exemption, makes a system high-risk.

title: GDPR Article 35 — Data Protection Impact Assessment
text:
# GDPR Article 35 — Data Protection Impact Assessment

**Date:** May 25, 2018
**Author:** Official Journal (consolidated)

Article 35 GDPR requires a data protection impact assessment where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. It sets when a data protection impact assessment is required and is the statutory basis from which internal data-protection policies derive their DPIA screening thresholds.

title: EDPB Guidelines — International Transfers and Transfer Tools

# EDPB Guidelines — International Transfers and Transfer Tools

**Date:** June 20, 2025
**Author:** European Data Protection Board

Supports — but does not itself set — an organisation's internal transfer policy.
